cards.q: On a turn-around at an outstation a CCM (the SCCM) reports feeling ill but says they feel well enough to operate their door for take-off and landing. 160 pax on board. How do you proceed and what considerations apply?
cards.a:
Do NOT accept self-assessment. (Refs: OM-A 6.1 / 8.3.14.5 / 4.2.1.4)

• OM-A 6.1: a crew member with reduced medical fitness that affects assigned duties shall not operate.
• As this is the SCCM, the SCCM must contact MedAire immediately, notify the Commander and Crew Services. Only MedAire determines fitness — not the crew member or Commander.
• If SCCM declared unfit (8.3.14.5b): the deputy (nominated at base briefing) takes over SCCM function until a replacement is provided or the aircraft returns to base.
• Minimum cabin crew (4.2.1.4): reduction allowed only if departing an outstation, ratio of at least 1 cabin crew per 50 pax (or fraction) on the same deck is kept, deputy SCCM adjusts service for cabin safety, and Commander is informed and agrees.

Required actions: written approval from NOC/Crew Services before departure; deputy SCCM takes over and briefs new seating; relocate pax by vacant crew seats; identify/brief an ABP for the affected exit; Commander files an ASR; deputy SCCM files a CSR.

Key Point: Medical fitness beats schedule. With 160 pax the 1:50 minimum complement ratio must still be met.

cards.q: Early departure: APU was left running so block FOB is less than requested. You have the OFP Take-Off fuel figure and topping up will cause a significant delay. What do you do?
cards.a:
Check it against minimum block fuel first. (Refs: OM-A 8.3.7.1 / 8.1.7.x)

Step 1 — Minimum Block Fuel (8.3.7.1): shall not commence unless PLANNED MIN is on board = taxi + trip + contingency + alternate (if req) + final reserve + additional.
Step 2 — Extra fuel (8.1.7.2.8): a buffer above minimum block fuel for company needs (GND/APU, HOLD ATC, HOLD WXX, EN WXX, TNK, MISC); it is NOT part of minimum block fuel.
Critical check: if current FOB ≥ PLANNED MIN → legal to depart; the APU simply burned the Extra Fuel buffer.

If short of minimum block fuel, compensation measures: single-engine taxi out (RETO ≈ 7 kg/min saved), closer runway, direct taxi routing, NOC flight-plan optimisation, optimal flight level, dynamic CI via Jeppesen FD Pro.

Decision: FOB ≥ PLANNED MIN → depart. If a shortfall remains and measures cover it → amend OFP, document, depart; if not → request uplift, accept delay.

Key Point: Commander has final authority on fuel. Consumed fuel is only a problem if it ate into PLANNED MIN.

cards.q: APU is unserviceable on a hot day and TAS wants to start boarding. Outline the Etihad boarding procedure regarding cabin temperature, what else you can do to reduce it, and other considerations.
cards.a:
Refs: OM-A 8.2.2.7 / 8.3.8.13 / FCTM PR-NP-SP-30.

Temperature rule (8.2.2.7): ideal boarding cabin temp is 20–28°C and must be within range before boarding starts.

Before boarding: GPU for electrical power (essential); ACU/pre-conditioned air for cooling (essential); verify 20–28°C; confirm ground equipment connected and working.

To reduce cabin temp (8.3.8.13 hot weather): close ALL window shades; open additional doors for cross-ventilation; set A/C target 23–24°C; minimise cabin lighting and delay IFE; request early ground-equipment connection.

Other considerations: MEL implications of APU U/S; engine start needs external pneumatic source; passenger comms via cabin crew; slower boarding pace (each pax ≈ 100 W body heat); document in ATL and coordinate with engineering.

Key Point: Without APU on a hot day, GPU + ACU are essential. If cooling can't hold 20–28°C, boarding shall not commence until safe.

cards.q: Your neighbour is travelling on a web-fare ticket and wants a jump seat. Is this permitted?
cards.a:
NO — not permitted. (Refs: OM-A 8.3.13 / 8.3.13.1 / 8.3.13.2 / 8.3.13.4)

Jump seats are authorised for certain categories only, and it is always the Commander's sole final decision who is accepted.

Permitted categories include: Etihad CEO/C-level execs; Authority Inspectors (official capacity); Etihad Quality Auditors (in-flight audits); Etihad GCAA-licensed flight/cabin crew; SFIs on observation flights; Flight Ops Officers (FOO); loadmasters on freighters; task specialists on duty; technical staff (cabin jump seat only); anyone with one-off NPH Flight Operations approval.

Requirements (8.3.13.4): authorised category; company ID or NPH approval; qualifies as ABP; must not distract crew; no alcohol.

Key Point: A regular web-fare passenger cannot use a jump seat. The neighbour uses their booked cabin seat.

cards.q: Which document confirms the procedure for carrying falcons on board, where is it kept, and where are falcons carried?
cards.a:
Refs: OM-A 8.2.3.8 / 8.2.3.8.1 / 8.2.3.8.3.

Document: Operations Manual Part A (OM-A), Ch 8.2 Ground Handling — 8.2.3.8 'Live Animals in the Cabin' and 8.2.3.8.1 'Falcons'.
Where kept: electronically on the EFB / Comply365 ('My Publications – Manuals – OM-A'); accessible on the flight deck at all times.

Where carried (8.2.3.8.1) — passenger cabin, conditions: max 15 falcons on scheduled flights (waived for VIP/charter); hooded at all times with light chain to legs and seat structure; last row of the booked class; protective plastic sheeting over floor/adjacent seat; perches tied down for large numbers; falcons not placed on seats.

Segregation if other animals: falcons & pets not same class, min 10 rows apart; falcons & service dogs min 10 rows apart; falcons with falcons — no segregation.

Key Point: Commander notified via NOTOC code PET; ground staff tells SCCM before boarding, SCCM informs Commander.

cards.q: During boarding a young passenger is reported with an outbreak of red spots resembling chicken pox. What do you do?
cards.a:
Don't diagnose — gather info, use MedLink. (Refs: OM-A 8.2.6.1.7.2 / 8.2.7 / 8.3.15.9.1; SEPM 4.4)

Step 1: red spots could be chicken pox, allergy, eczema, heat rash or bites. Have crew/SCCM speak discreetly with the parent about diagnosis, doctor visits, certificates, symptoms, vaccination status and contacts.
Step 2 — station: at AUH contact MedLink via ground staff (EAMC available, easier rebooking); at an outstation contact MedLink immediately, possibly local health authority, coordinate NOC for re-accommodation.
Step 3 — if communicable suspected/confirmed (8.2.6.1.7.2): a medical certificate stating the disease would not be communicable in flight is required, dated within 10 days; if none and MedLink advises against travel, do not accept.
Step 4 — Commander's authority (8.2.7): may refuse carriage if condition is a safety/security risk or a hazard to others.

Offload (8.2.7.1): SCCM arranges offload and discreetly escorts pax; ground staff advise reason and offload baggage; security check of accessed areas; SCCM raises CSR, Commander files iReport.

Key Point: All passengers' wellbeing comes first. Chicken pox is airborne and highly contagious. Rely on MedLink — don't diagnose.

cards.q: A passenger has gastroenteritis, was examined by a doctor at an outstation, was prescribed medication, and wants to travel. Would you allow it? Who might you contact?
cards.a:
Yes — allow travel. (Refs: OM-A 8.2.6.1.7.2 / 8.2.7.2)

Assessment: already examined by a qualified doctor, prescribed medication, not incapacitated, wishes to travel — no indication of active unfitness.
Decision (8.2.7.2): if a passenger insists they are fit-to-fly they may be accepted, travelling at their own risk and without further questioning, unless they pose a risk to others' health/safety.

Practical measures: inform SCCM for discreet monitoring; seat near a lavatory if possible; crew ready to assist; if it deteriorates in flight, contact MedLink.
Who to contact if needed: MedLink (deterioration/doubt); CRO if available (handling disputes); NOC (operational coordination).

Key Point: Final decision rests with the Commander. With a medical assessment obtained and the pax willing, there's no reasonable basis to refuse.

cards.q: A lady boarding is reported as pregnant. What are your concerns as Captain and what procedure do you follow?
cards.a:
Refs: OM-A 8.2.6.2 (Expectant Mothers) / 8.3.15.10 (Birth on Board).

Concerns: stage of pregnancy / within permitted window; required certificate (if applicable); risk of complications or birth on board (esp. long-haul); safety/wellbeing of all.
Procedure: appoint a female crew member to discreetly view any certificate and ascertain weeks of pregnancy.

Single pregnancy: 0–28 wks no documents; 29–36 wks medical certificate; 37 wks+ not permitted.
Multiple pregnancy: 0–28 wks no documents; 29–32 wks medical certificate; 33 wks+ not permitted.

Certificate must: be on official letterhead or Etihad form; be signed by doctor/midwife with details/stamp; be valid within 21 days of issue; state fit to fly, single/multiple, weeks and EDD; be in English or Arabic.

Key Point: If the certificate lacks info, MedLink may clear. At 37+ wks (single) or 33+ wks (multiple) travel is not permitted.

cards.q: A properly cased, unloaded sporting rifle is being loaded into the hold. The TAS has no NOTOC and says it'll take an hour to generate one. What do you do?
cards.a:
NOTOC is mandatory — do not load without it. (Refs: OM-A 9.2.1.2 / 9.2.1.4 / 9.2.2.1 / 9.2.3 / 9.1.13)

A sporting rifle = Sporting Weapon (SWP); cased and unloaded satisfies 9.2.1.4. Per 9.2.3 weapons/ammunition in the hold SHALL be reflected on the NOTOC (as Firearms in Baggage, FAM); per 9.1.13 the Commander must be provided a NOTOC and cannot accept the shipment without a signed one.

Verify prerequisites: TAC approval (9.2.2.1); security permits for dep/arr/transit (9.2.4); firearm in locked container with key/combo restricted to the passenger; firearm unloaded (confirmed).
Decision on the 1-hour delay: (A) wait for NOTOC if delay acceptable (FDP/curfew/slot ok); (B) depart without the rifle if not, offload for next flight. Either way, never accept without a NOTOC.
Alternative (9.1.13): TAS confirms details verbally and arranges a preliminary NOTOC via ACARS; final NOTOC sent in flight before arrival.

Key Point: The Commander can't sign for what isn't documented. No NOTOC, no load — wait or use preliminary NOTOC via ACARS.

cards.q: What are the general limitations on Last Minute Changes (LMC) to a loadsheet, and when are transit bags allowed to be carried?
cards.a:
Refs: OM-A 8.1.8.6 / 8.1.8.6.1 / 10.6.6; GOM 10.3.2.

Part 1 — LMC: changes after release of the final loadsheet. LMC are NOT permitted to the ACARS loadsheet or to fuel figures.
LMC limits (8.1.8.6.1): Narrow body 500 kg; Wide body 1000 kg.
Standard weights: combined pax/baggage 100 kg; hand-baggage to cargo 7 kg/piece; if actual bag weight unknown 15 kg/bag; heavy items (mobility/camera) actual weight; cargo/mail/EIC actual weight.
Who may perform: Etihad flight crew, holders of a valid Etihad load-control licence, or CLC Coordinators at network airports.

Part 2 — Transit bags (10.6.6 / GOM 10.3.2): principle is passenger-baggage reconciliation. Permitted if screened, reconciled with a passenger confirmed on the flight, and compliant with security/handling. If a transit pax fails to board: offload the unaccompanied bag, update the Hold Baggage Manifest, inform Commander all bags are offloaded.

Key Point: LMC can't touch ACARS loadsheets or fuel figures; over tolerance → new loadsheet. Transit bags only when reconciled with confirmed passengers.

cards.q: A +400 kg block fuel error is spotted on a wide-body loadsheet. Can the TAS or Captain correct it by LMC?
cards.a:
No — cannot be corrected by LMC. (Refs: OM-A 8.1.8.6 / 8.1.8.6.1)

A block fuel error is a fuel-figure discrepancy. LMC are not permitted to ACARS loadsheets or fuel figures — regardless of magnitude. This is a blanket prohibition, not a tolerance question. (Even if it were traffic load, the wide-body LMC tolerance is 1000 kg — but irrelevant, since fuel figures can't be amended by LMC at all.)

Required action: issue a new loadsheet with the correct block fuel; TAS contacts load control for a revised loadsheet.

Key Point: Don't accept a loadsheet with an incorrect fuel figure — it affects TOW, LW and trim. A new loadsheet is mandatory.

cards.q: What items must be checked on a PDI each time an aircraft is on a turnaround?
cards.a:
Refs: OM-A 8.2.2.4 / 8.1.11.3 / 8.1.11.4.1.1 / 10.3.1.2.

1) Exterior walk-around (8.2.2.4): by an operating flight crew member, not delegated. Check pitot/static ports not damaged/obstructed; flight controls not locked/disabled; no frost/snow/ice on critical surfaces; no structural damage; per OM-B, wearing hi-vis vest.
2) ATL review (8.1.11.4.1.1): applicable NTCs and FCTNs; all open defects actioned/deferred per MEL/CDL; apply MEL/CDL procedures; validity of Transit/Daily/ETOPS checks for the whole flight; DDL validity; enough fuel; CRS signed; sign Commander's Acceptance.
3) Maintenance checks (8.1.11.3): Transit before every departure; Daily within 48 h of engineer sign-off; ETOPS before every ETOPS flight (if applicable).
4) Security check (10.3.1.2): cabin, cargo hold (by authorised ground rep), and exterior (wheel wells, fuselage, service panels).

Key Point: PDI = exterior inspection + ATL review + maintenance-check validity + security checks. Commander signs acceptance only when fully satisfied with airworthiness.

cards.q: What may the Commander assume when the SCCM reports 'Cabin Ready' before departure?
cards.a:
Refs: OM-A 8.3.15.3 / 8.3.15.2.

May assume (8.3.15.3): all pax have had the required safety briefing/demo; the entire cabin (occupants, galleys, lavatories) is secured against strong movement/acceleration; all cabin crew are seated and secured as required.

Specific checks completed (8.3.15.2) include: doors closed and slides armed; announcements/demos done; pax seated, belts fastened, seat backs up, armrests down; tables/handsets/IFE stowed; infants secured (belt or CRD); no-smoking observed; carry-ons secured; overhead/compartments closed/locked; bassinets stowed; aisles/exit rows/exits clear; door window blinds open/clear; galleys/equipment stowed, galley electrics off (except fridges/chillers); lavatories clear and locked; lighting matched to outside; ISPSS off, large PEDs stowed; dividers/curtains secured open; self-help exit briefing confirmed; crew seated.

Key Point: 'Cabin Secure' is given ~3–5 min before take-off; flight crew then PA 'Cabin Crew – seats for departure.'

cards.q: List the contents of the aircraft library. If the ICAO 'Emergency Response Guidance for Aircraft Incidents Involving Dangerous Goods' (Doc 9481) appears missing, can you depart?
cards.a:
Refs: OM-A 8.1.12 / 8.1.12.1 / 8.1.12.2 / 9.1.14.2.

Aircraft documents (8.1.12.1): original C of Registration; original C of Airworthiness; original Airworthiness Review Certificate; Noise Certificate; certified true copy of the AOC; associated Ops Specs for type; foreign Ops Specs if required; original Aircraft Radio Licence; Certificate of Insurance; ATL; Cabin Maintenance Log; DG Operator's Certificate; other regulatory approvals.
Manuals (8.1.12.2): OM-A, OM-B, OM-C; SEPM; FAOM (freighter only); DG Emergency Response Guide (ICAO Doc 9481); Security procedures (OM-A 10); GOM.

Can you depart if Doc 9481 is missing? YES — per 9.1.14.2 it's available electronically on Comply365 (Collections/Manuals/Dangerous Goods Guide Doc 9481). Verify electronic access before departure. If BOTH physical and electronic are unavailable → NO; obtain a copy or contact MCC.

Key Point: Electronic format is acceptable (8.1.12). Verify EFB access before departure if the physical copy is missing.

cards.q: What are the altimeter error limits on the A350 — between main altimeters on the ground/in flight, entering RVSM airspace, and the standby altimeter?
cards.a:
Authoritative table: A350 FCOM PRO-SPO-RVSM P1/4. (Also OM-A 8.3.2.4.5/.6/.7; AFM NORM-34)

On ground (8.3.2.4.7): between primary altimeters ±20 ft; primary vs airport elevation ±75 ft.
Prior to / in RVSM (8.3.2.4.5): between primary altimeters ±200 ft (±60 m), incl. hourly crosscheck in RVSM; level change overshoot/undershoot 150 ft (45 m).
RVSM equipment (A350, AFM NORM-34): 2 ADR; 1 ATC transponder; 1 FWS (altitude alert); 1 autopilot; 2 PFD; 1 AFS Control Panel.
Contingency — notify ATC immediately (8.3.2.4.6) if in RVSM and: deviation >200 ft (±60 m); loss of altimetry redundancy; all autopilots fail; altimeter discrepancy with no way to tell which is correct; turbulence more than moderate.

Key Point: For the complete authoritative max-difference table, refer to A350 FCOM PRO-SPO-RVSM P1/4.

cards.q: The TAS asks for the fuel docket and you wish to amend the figures. Should you prepare a new one?
cards.a:
Yes — for an electronic (ACARS) fuel docket, send a new one with amended figures. (Refs: OM-A 8.1.8.4 / 8.1.8.6)

Fuel docket contents (8.1.8.4): Trip fuel (per OFP); Taxi fuel (per OFP); Block fuel (FOB at pushback = block minus ground usage); RTOW (or certified MTOW if N/A); OFP No.; ID (PIC staff number).

Amendment method: Fuel docket (electronic/ACARS) → send a new docket with corrected figures. Loadsheet fuel figures → cannot be amended (LMC not permitted) → new loadsheet required.
Note: the fuel docket is a crew-prepared document; per OM-A 8.1.7 the Commander has final authority on fuel carried.

Key Point: Unlike the loadsheet (fuel figures can't be amended by LMC), the fuel docket is crew-prepared — send a new one with corrected figures.

cards.q: There are insufficient meals loaded for passengers. What is the company policy on delaying a flight for late meals?
cards.a:
No specific OM-A policy exists on delaying for late/insufficient pax meals. (Refs: OM-A 8.2.2.17 / 8.2.2.18)

General principle: flights should not be delayed for catering shortfalls alone.
Rationale: catering is a commercial/service matter, not safety; Etihad prioritises OTP; 8.2.2.18 — all efforts to achieve delay recovery; extended-delay policy — if pax on board 2+ hours, food/snacks shall be provided; the decision to delay is coordinated with NOC.

Commander considerations: flight duration (short vs long-haul comfort); time of day/meal relevance; premium-cabin expectations; how long to load meals; knock-on effects (FDP, curfews, connections, slots).
Actions: coordinate with SCCM on the shortfall and alternatives; inform NOC for the commercial decision; brief crew to manage expectations; don't delay for minor shortfalls; for significant long-haul shortfalls, NOC decides.

Key Point: The Commander's job is safe, efficient operation. Catering shortfalls are a service issue, not safety — NOC makes commercial delay calls.

cards.q: A passenger wishes to use his own oxygen cylinder for medical purposes. Where should it be stowed and what procedure applies?
cards.a:
A passenger may NOT use their own oxygen cylinder. (Refs: OM-A 8.2.6.1.6 / OM-A 9; SEPM 4.9.1/4.9.2)

Own cylinder — not permitted: medical-use oxygen cylinders must not exceed 5 kg gross and need Etihad MEDA clearance (this refers to company-arranged oxygen). Personal devices containing liquid oxygen are prohibited.
Company-provided 'ZERO TWO' units: for pre-diagnosed pax who advise at reservation; company arranges bottles with prior medical clearance; a Crew Member Alert (CMA) is issued with bottle count and flow rate; loading/storing/securing/operating per SEPM 4.9.1.
FAA-approved POCs: permitted in the cabin if stowed safely; pax must carry battery for 1.5× flight time (150%); approved list in SEPM 4.9.2. Ventilators/respirators/CPAP also allowed if stowable.

Summary: own O2 cylinder NO; liquid-oxygen device prohibited; ZERO TWO YES (MEDA clearance, CMA); FAA POC YES (150% battery); aircraft emergency O2 NOT for pax medical use.

Key Point: Aircraft onboard oxygen (safety equipment) is never used for pax medical purposes. Pax need advance medical clearance and use ZERO TWO units or approved POCs.

cards.q: A group of visually impaired passengers board with several guide dogs. Is it OK for the dogs to travel in the cabin? What if the aircraft is full?
cards.a:
Yes — guide dogs (service dogs) are permitted in the cabin. (Refs: OM-A 8.2.3.8.2 / 8.2.3.8.3 / 8.2.6.1.3)

Conditions (8.2.3.8.2): accompanying pax at least 18; never separated from the dog; SVAN added to the PNR; pre-boarding allowed; pax provides food and absorbent mat; dog leashed/harnessed/tethered at all times.
Seating: preferred bulkhead and/or window; NOT in emergency exit rows, nor one row fwd/aft of over-wing exits.

Limit on number (8.2.3.8.3): no limit to service dogs on a flight, provided the number of pax travelling with a service dog does not exceed the number of ABPs able to assist an evacuation.
Aircraft full: they must still be accommodated; no occupancy-based limit applies; seating adjustments may be needed.

Key Point: Service dogs for visually impaired pax are always permitted in the cabin with no numerical limit, even when full — the only constraint is enough ABPs for evacuation. Exit-row seating restrictions apply.

cards.q: A VIP is travelling with a police escort, and a policeman is carrying a pistol for security. Can this be allowed?
cards.a:
Yes — but only if specific conditions are met. (Refs: OM-A 9.2.2.2 / 9.2.3)

Who may carry firearms/ammunition in the cabin with prior TAC approval (9.2.2.2): UAE police escorting UAE Royal family/ministers/VVIPs; protection officers of an authorised foreign government official; IFSO / Air Marshals.
Ammunition: authorised armed personnel may carry both firearm AND ammunition in the cabin with TAC approval (differs from checked baggage, where firearm and ammo are in separate containers).

Mandatory requirements: Individual Application for Carriage of Firearm/s approved by EY AVSEC TAC; signed Authorised Carriage of Firearms Notice; SCCM notified before boarding; SCCM presents boarding pass to Commander (names, seats, number of firearms); SCCM discreetly ensures armed pax are aware of one another; armed pax briefed on rules/risks; firearms/ammo concealed at all times; no alcohol service.
NOTOC: firearms/ammunition in the cabin do NOT need to be on the NOTOC; Commander notified per 9.2.2.2.

Key Point: Allowed only with prior TAC approval, all signed documentation, Commander and SCCM notified before departure, and all procedures followed.

cards.q: A teenage passenger playing a Nintendo is clearly annoying other passengers. How do you deal with it?
cards.a:
Graduated response. (Refs: OM-A 10.6.10.2 / 10.6.10.2.1 / 10.6.10.2.4 / 8.3.15.7.1)

The Nintendo (PED) is permitted, but the behaviour is a disturbance.
Step 1 — polite de-escalation (10.6.10.2): explain the gaming is disturbing others.
Step 2 — request compliance: lower volume / use headphones, move seat if available, or take a break.
Step 3 — verbal warning if non-compliant (10.6.10.2.1): SCCM issues a positive instruction focused on the behaviour, not the person.
Step 4 — Commander's authority (8.3.15.7.1): the Commander may order PEDs switched off and stowed for any operational, security or safety reason.
Complaints (10.6.10.2.4): a complaint against another passenger shall be documented by the crew for reference.

Key Point: Polite conversation, then verbal warning; Commander can order the device off. Avoid physical confrontation; goal is to restore cabin order.

cards.q: What is company policy on passengers with reduced mobility and seating near exit rows?
cards.a:
PRMs shall NOT be seated in exit rows. (Refs: OM-A 8.2.5.3 / 8.2.6.1.5)

Exit-row seats are for ABPs only — pax who appear reasonably fit, strong and able to assist a rapid evacuation after briefing.
Prohibited from exit rows (8.2.5.3): can't understand English/the briefing; obvious physical/mental disability affecting quick movement; substantially blind or deaf; too frail (age/sickness) to move quickly; so obese they'd struggle to move/reach an exit; under 18; travelling with animals; deportees/inadmissibles/persons in custody; pregnant women.

PRM seating guidance (8.2.6.1.5): when practical give max space; plaster casts must not obstruct aisle/exits; crutches/canes/aids stored within quick reach; one-sided disability — unaffected side toward aisle; groups of PRMs in subgroups for rapid evacuation flow.

Key Point: PRMs are categorically barred from exit-row seats — a safety requirement so pax near exits can assist a rapid evacuation.

cards.q: A diplomatic mailbag is brought to the flight deck just before departure. Can you carry it?
cards.a:
It depends — only if HOC conditions are met. (Refs: OM-A 10.5.2 / 8.2.3.11.4)

A diplomatic pouch may be carried as a Hand of Crew (HOC) item only if (10.5.2): accompanied by a signed Hand of Crew shipment form; screened to ensure no prohibited items; intact, not damaged or tampered with.
Commander notification: the SCCM (or loadmaster on freighters) shall inform the Commander of HOC carriage before departure.
Critical issue — screening: under the Vienna Convention diplomatic bags are generally inviolable, but from an aviation-security view unscreened items cannot be accepted.

Key Point: Carry it only if it meets all HOC requirements — signed form, screened, intact. If not screened (even claiming diplomatic immunity), the Commander should refuse.

cards.q: A passenger has boarded clearly intoxicated but peaceful. Would you offload or carry him?
cards.a:
Commander's discretion based on risk. (Refs: OM-A 10.6.10.1 / 10.5.5 / 8.2.7)

Per 10.6.10.1, once a passenger has boarded, whether to carry rests with the Commander.
Considerations: current behaviour/compliance; level of intoxication (can they self-care and follow safety instructions?); risk of deterioration (alcohol effects intensify at altitude); flight duration; ability to self-evacuate.
Option A — carry (peaceful, cooperative, follows instructions): no alcohol service, crew monitoring, seat for easy monitoring.
Option B — offload: severe intoxication, significant deterioration risk, or unable to self-evacuate.

Key Point: No automatic requirement to offload a peaceful intoxicated pax — it's a risk-based Commander decision. But intoxication is an explicit offload criterion; if in doubt, the safer course is to offload.

cards.q: An intoxicated passenger is causing a verbal disturbance prior to doors closing. What would you do?
cards.a:
Offload. (Refs: OM-A 8.2.7.1 / 10.5.5 / 10.6.10.1)

Two compounding factors — intoxication AND verbal disturbance — both are independent offload criteria (10.5.5).
Course of action: SCCM informs Commander immediately; attempt to defuse (polite but firm, remind of Conditions of Carriage); Commander decides to offload (high in-flight escalation risk).
Offload (8.2.7.1): SCCM has ground staff facilitate; SCCM discreetly escorts pax to ground staff; ground staff advise the reason; checked baggage offloaded; security check of accessed areas; SCCM raises CSR.
If pax refuses — call police; staff shall never attempt to arrest or physically detain.

Key Point: Offload — multiple criteria are met and in-flight escalation risk is high. Doors open means the problem can be removed safely now.

cards.q: Can a Commander refuse to carry a passenger prior to doors closing?
cards.a:
Yes. (Refs: OM-A 8.2.7 / 10.5.5)

Authority to offload (10.5.5): pax still outside the aircraft → ground staff authority; pax already boarded → Commander authority.
Commander authority (8.2.7) — may refuse/offload if, in his opinion, the person's conduct/status/age/condition: renders him unsuitable for safety/security; causes discomfort or is objectionable to others; is physically unfit for air travel; shows behaviour consistent with intoxication; is a hazard to self/others/property/aircraft; involves disorderly/abusive behaviour and a physical threat; fails to obey lawful crew/official instructions.

Key Point: Yes. Once a pax has boarded, offload authority rests with the Commander — but he must not discriminate against passengers with disabilities.

cards.q: Is there any significance in having the doors closed regarding the Commander's authority to accept or refuse passengers?
cards.a:
Yes — door closure has major legal/operational significance. (Refs: OM-A 10.6.10 / 8.3.12.1.1; Tokyo Convention 1963)

Definition link (10.6.10): an unruly/disruptive passenger is defined by acts committed 'from the moment the aircraft door is closed prior to take-off to the moment it is reopened after landing.'
Before vs after closure: offload — available before / requires return to stand or diversion after; ground staff and police access — available before / not until landing after; options — simple offload before / warning, restraint or diversion only after; cost/disruption — minimal before / significant after.
Flight-deck security (8.3.12.1.1): the flight-deck door must be closed and locked from when all external doors are closed after embarkation until reopened for disembarkation.

Key Point: Door closure marks the start of the Commander's enhanced legal authority under international conventions, triggers flight-deck security, and removes the simple offload option — so act decisively on passenger concerns BEFORE doors close.

cards.q: The ground engineer's headset fails just before pushback. How can you proceed with the pushback?
cards.a:
Use an agreed alternative — primarily hand signals. (Refs: A350 MEL 23-51-02A; OM-A 8.2.1.6.1 / 12.7; GOM 5.4)

Per MEL 23-51-02A: cockpit-to-ground comms shall be via hand signals (per the GOM) after consultation with the attending ground engineer.
Other agreed means (8.2.1.6.1): hand signals (primary); phone call to ground staff via NOC/Ground Handling relaying to the engineer/tug driver; service interphone if available; any other suitable agreed means.
Procedure: agree the method with the engineer; if hand signals, keep visual contact throughout; if phone relay, establish a clear protocol before starting pushback.

Key Point: A headset failure doesn't prevent pushback — use hand signals per the GOM, or a phone relay via NOC/Ground Handling, after consulting the ground engineer.

cards.q: A prisoner is to be transported with a police escort and the TAS wants to fuel and board at the same time. Should the prisoner be pre-boarded?
cards.a:
Yes — boarded first. (Refs: OM-A 8.2.6.4 / 8.2.1.6)

Boarding/disembarking persons in custody (8.2.6.4): ground staff inform the SCCM as early as possible, who informs the Commander; persons in custody are boarded first and disembarked last (does not apply to INAD/Overstay pax).
Simultaneous fuelling and boarding does not change the sequence — the prisoner is still boarded first.
Additional: seating in rear-most seats, not adjacent to exits, block the row in front when possible; minimum 2 escorts, one same gender/language as the escortee; escorts handle security/behaviour, search the seat/surroundings, and retain travel documents (DEPA/EINAD).
Commander's discretion: may refuse to carry persons in custody or impose extra restrictions if their carriage raises safety/security risk.

Key Point: Yes — pre-board the prisoner (first on, last off), in rear-most seats away from exits, per OM-A 8.2.6.4.
